documents: Hatfield, Elliott, Wyatt, Xie & Zumberge (2022), Results From a Decade of Optical Fiber Strainmeters at Piñon Flat Observatory, Earth and Space Science 9, e2022EA002381 (published PDF, 11 pages)

entry.evidence: offer an inexpensive and robust means to observe Earth strain

steps.action: Describe the optical fiber strainmeter principle: interferometric measurement of a sensing fiber against a reference fiber, with equal-arm interferometers to suppress laser wavelength noise.
steps.quote: We monitor length changes in our OFSs with optical interferometry.

steps.action: Use the 251-m borehole OFS (BOFS), built and described in the authors' earlier work, as one of the three sensors.
steps.quote: Our 251-m deep borehole OFS, described by DeWolf et al. (2015), has been operating since 2012 at our test site

steps.action: Build trench OFSs (174 m NWSE, 221 m EW) with a second, thermally contrasting fiber for temperature correction and, on NWSE, optical anchors tying the endpoints to 10 m depth.
steps.quote: which link the near-surface measurement to deeper material

steps.action: Record bidirectional fiber length changes with the quadrature fringe resolution method from the authors' earlier work (0.52 nε per radian for 174 m at 1310 nm).
steps.quote: The method of quadrature fringe resolution described in Zumberge et al. (2004) and DeWolf et al. (2015) is used

steps.action: Set the acquisition at 50 kHz phase sampling decimated to 20 sps, and a procedure for editing gaps and steps by extrapolating the pre-gap slope.
steps.quote: Gaps that do occur must be edited by estimating the slope of the record leading up to the gap

steps.action: Record temperature at the surface and at 0.5, 1 and 1.5 m depth at PFO and estimate the diurnal attenuation (54 dB per m), establishing thermal noise as the key difficulty.
steps.quote: Figure 3 shows the temperature recorded at several depths at PFO.

steps.action: Estimate the temperature correction coefficients (fiber-pair difference and mandrel thermistor) from laboratory values adjusted by least squares on the field record.
steps.quote: The coefficients are determined in the lab and adjusted by least squares to minimize the impact of temperature changes on the record.

steps.action: After the first TOFS-NWSE installation's optical anchor signals failed to match near-surface noise, re-excavate, test, and redesign the anchor mounts to sit in line with the sensing-cable termination.
steps.quote: Many months of observations revealed that the optical anchor signals did not match well the noise from the presumed near-surface strains.

steps.action: Record and fully correct a 2-month TOFS-NWSE strain series (temperature and anchor corrections, with mandrel temperature control off), giving 19.5 nε RMS after removing a 778 nε per month slope.
steps.quote: The RMS variation of the fully corrected strain record over this 2-month interval is 19.5 nε.

steps.action: Compare the corrected TOFS-NWSE record with the parallel 732 m vacuum laser strainmeter and conclude that the ±20 nε residuals are instrument artifacts, which sets the detection limit.
steps.quote: This informs us that the residual strains from TOFS-NWSE are instrument artifacts and not real earth strain signals.

steps.action: Record 2-month series for TOFS-EW (174 nε RMS, noise attributed to shallow 2 m rod monuments) and BOFS (5.4 nε RMS), and compare all three sensors in Figure 5.
steps.quote: The RMS strain over this time period after a removal of 98 nε per month drift is 174 nε.

steps.action: List candidate sources of the residual noise: the reference mandrel fibers versus the sensing fiber, and lateral variations in the cable path.
steps.quote: Noting the different residual noise among the three sensors we have considered a number of possible sources.

steps.action: Test reference fibers on mandrels: two 200 m fibers on one mandrel over 32 days (0.74 nε RMS), and a 500 m fiber measured by electronic distance meter over 24 years (stable to 100 nε per year).
steps.quote: Over a 32-day test in a thermally benign lab environment the apparent RMS strain was 0.74 nε.

steps.action: Compute the apparent strain a lateral cable-path disturbance would produce: 0.3 mm amplitude at 10 m wavelength gives 10 nε.
steps.quote: a sinusoidally varying lateral disturbance having amplitude 0.3 mm and wavelength 10 m

steps.action: Show the 9.5-year BOFS record with the annual cycle removed beside two well water-table records, note a possible correlation, and leave it unmodelled.
steps.quote: suggest that there is a possible correlation between water table and vertical strain

steps.action: Characterize the optical fiber anchors as shallow strainmeters over 2 years: monument drift below 0.1 mm per year, with corrections that matter after rain.
steps.quote: While designed only for corrections to TOFS-NWSE, the Optical Fiber Anchors (OFAs) are interesting in their own right as shallow strainmeters.

steps.action: Compare the tidal strains recorded by TOFS-NWSE with the parallel vacuum laser strainmeter, using 2-day high-passed data (Figure 8).
steps.quote: The OFSs display clearly the solid Earth tides and the amplitudes are in good agreement with recordings from the 730-m-long vacuum laser strainmeters.

steps.action: Estimate the OFS scale factor (0.96) that minimizes the difference from the vacuum strainmeter, leaving a residual of 2.6 nε RMS.
steps.quote: A scale factor of 0.96 applied to the OFS record minimizes the difference between the records.

steps.action: Re-estimate the scale factor from M2 tidal amplitudes (0.98) and attribute the difference to heterogeneity of the material along the two baselines.
steps.quote: comparing the amplitudes of the M2 tidal line gives a value of 0.98

steps.action: Derive the long-wavelength plane-wave approximation in which strain equals minus ground velocity divided by apparent velocity, so that seismometer records predict strainmeter records.
steps.quote: There is a very simple approximation for comparing strainmeter signals to seismometer outputs

steps.action: Compare OFS records of several earthquakes (two shown: Mw 8.2 Alaska, Mw 5.3 Santa Cruz Is.) with seismometer-derived strain in 0.01-1 Hz, finding matching waveforms and comparable SNR.
steps.quote: Using this simple approximation we compared several records from earthquakes with those from nearby seismometers at PFO

steps.action: Compare noise spectra of the OFSs with the PBO borehole strainmeter and a seismometer in February and July 2021, finding shared 0.1-0.3 Hz microseism peaks and seasonal changes consistent with Tanimoto et al. (2006).
steps.quote: Data recorded by all three techniques show similar peak frequencies between 0.1 and 0.3 Hz.

steps.action: Keep the claim that OFSs are useful seismic and tidal recorders and could detect slow-slip events of 100 nε and larger, citing low cost and wide dynamic range.
steps.quote: These comparisons suggest that the OFSs could serve as useful seismic recorders

steps.action: Propose, without trying it, a Galperin configuration of three directionally drilled angled boreholes to combine thermal isolation and competent rock.
steps.quote: One option we have considered but not yet tried is to make use of directional drilling to create three angled boreholes

tree.answer: Earth strain (tides, seismic waves, slow slip) recorded by long-baseline optical fiber strainmeters
Yes, interferometrically, after temperature and anchor corrections
Characterize OFS noise and performance, chiefly for slow-slip detection
Noise-source candidates only: thermal, reference mandrel, lateral cable path, monument motion
Partly: lateral path disturbance predicted at 10 nε; mandrel noise bounded by lab tests
Found: natural tides and earthquakes at PFO; lab mandrel tests set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: daily tides and several earthquakes repeat the comparison
Agreement with vacuum strainmeters, a seismometer and the PBO borehole strainmeter across two seasons
Capability characterized: about 20 nε noise (NWSE), tidal scale 0.96-0.98, seismic agreement in 0.01-1 Hz

end.claim: Trench and borehole optical fiber strainmeters record tides and seismic strain in agreement with reference instruments, with residual noise of about 20 nε (TOFS-NWSE) and drift up to 1 µε per month, so they could detect slow-slip events of 100 nε and larger.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparison with the collocated 732 m vacuum laser strainmeter shows the TOFS-NWSE residuals are instrument artifacts, which sets the ±20 nε detection limit and supports the tidal calibration.

gates.evidence: Data come from continuously running instruments; no stated hypothesis directed acquisition. The comparisons with vacuum strainmeters, a seismometer and the PBO borehole strainmeter could have failed (the vacuum comparison did expose residual artifacts), but the headline slow-slip capability is extrapolated from noise levels, not tested on a slow-slip event. Correction coefficients were adjusted by least squares on the same records; nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Michelson fiber interferometry with 3×3 couplers and Faraday mirrors (Li et al. 2016, a refractometer paper)
strain-optic coefficient of the fiber's index of refraction, used for calibration
electronic distance meter used to measure the 500 m reference fiber
commercial fiber with a contrasting temperature coefficient (Fibercore PS1250) in a K-Tube custom cable

novelty_claims.quote: The NWSE version's main improvement over earlier installations is the addition of “optical anchors”
Our borehole OFS is the longest running optical fiber sensor at PFO.

limits: No review file was supplied, so only the final-paper sequence is coded. The slow-slip detection claim is inferred from noise levels; no slow-slip event is recorded or tested. The source of the ±20 nε TOFS-NWSE residual is unidentified ('Further work is needed', p. 5). Only 2-month windows are shown, and why those windows were chosen is not stated (inference: possible selection of quiet intervals). Temperature-correction coefficients are tuned by least squares on the same records they correct (inference: risk of overfitting). Of 'a number of earthquakes', only two are shown. The lateral-path noise estimate is computed but not compared with data. Sub-claims: seismic-band agreement and tidal calibration (scale 0.96-0.98) are capability_characterized; the water-table/BOFS correlation has status none ('possible', not modelled); the Galperin configuration is a proposal only. TOFS-EW noise attributed to shallow monuments is a best_explanation without a direct test. The authors do not report how mandrel temperature control on versus off quantitatively changes noise ('debatably better').

disagreements.target: short-baseline borehole strainmeters (baselines of the order of a borehole diameter)
disagreements.support: The paper argues that long baselines reduce strain noise and sensitivity to grout microcracks; no direct test is offered beyond the spectral comparison with the PBO borehole strainmeter.
disagreements.quote: Short strainmeters whose baselines are of the order of a borehole diameter can be subject to spurious signals from very localized displacements

disagreements.target: GNSS antenna pairs for detecting localized strain
disagreements.support: A sensitivity argument: detecting 100 nε needs mm precision over tens of km, which prevents localizing sources; no GNSS data are analysed.
disagreements.quote: prohibiting localizing the strain signals within several km of the source

alternatives_considered.alternatives: unequal-arm interferometer with an auxiliary wavelength-monitoring interferometer (BOFS)
alternatives_considered.reason: equal-arm designs are insensitive to laser wavelength fluctuations and allow inexpensive laser diodes

alternatives_considered.alternatives: 2 m driven steel rods without optical anchoring (TOFS-EW)
alternatives_considered.reason: to correct and stabilize the endpoints against near-surface thermoelastic displacement
smaller short-term corrections, debatably better performance in the days-to-weeks band

alternatives_considered.chosen: either the local buried reference fiber or the deep borehole mandrel, by band
alternatives_considered.alternatives: local buried reference fiber; reference mandrel at the bottom of the borehole
alternatives_considered.reason: the local reference is better for short-period noise, the deep reference for long-period noise owing to its thermal stability

alternatives_considered.alternatives: three angled directionally drilled boreholes in a Galperin configuration (not tried)
alternatives_considered.reason: trenches are cheaper but perform worse; a Galperin configuration would combine thermal isolation, competent rock, and the full strain field
